new_statements.quote: d) Der dynamische Ton liegt, soviel ich sehe, auf der vorletzten Silbe. Musikalischen Ton glaube ich beobachtet zu haben in khónthuma »er sendet mich« und kho̱nthuma »du sendest mich«. Das erstere hat, soviel ich meine gehört zu haben, hohen Ton. Der Sprecher reißt dabei die Augen auf und wirft den Kopf etwas hintenüber. [p.102:] ko, 2. Pers. Sing, und ko Kl. 1 unterscheiden sich nur durch die Tonhöhe.
new_statements.translation: d) The dynamic accent [stress] lies, as far as I can see, on the penultimate syllable. Musical [pitch] tone I believe I have observed in khónthuma 'he sends me' and kho̱nthuma 'you send me'. The former has, as far as I think I heard, high tone; the speaker opens his eyes wide and throws his head back a little. [p.102:] ko (2nd person singular) and ko (class 1) differ only in pitch.

Der Sprecher reißt dabei die Augen auf und wirft den Kopf etwas hintenüber.' (scanned line 49799ff matches; only the tone diacritics on khonthuma are scanned-garbled). The supp…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress ('dynamischer Ton') falls on the penultimate syllable; Meinhof hedges ('soviel ich sehe') and reports residual pitch distinctions only for a couple of verb-prefix contrasts (3sg vs 2sg subject ka-/ku- + object, cl.1 ko vs 2sg ko).
new_statements.exceptions: Only the pitch (not stress) contrasts khónthuma vs kho̱nthuma and ko (2sg) vs ko (cl.1); aspiration kh is confined to the stem syllable (p.90) and a pretonic o 'weit von der Tonsilbe entfernt' is less open (p.91). No stress exceptions listed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement based on elicitation with Pastor Holst (1900) and speakers from Dar es Salaam, Kisarawe and Maneromango (1902); no distinction drawn between citation forms and phrasal context. Consistent with later comparative remarks that East Ruvu languages incl. Zaramo have lost tonal distinctiveness and share areal penultimate stress with Swahili (Nurse & Hinnebusch 1993: 248, 524, 558; Hyman 2017).
new_statements.identity_note: Meinhof 1907 describes 'Dzalamo' as spoken at Dar es Salaam, Kisarawe (Kisalawe) and Maneromango, i.e. Zaramo proper = zara1247 (he notes the spelling Zaramo arises from young speakers' l > r). Nurse 1979 spells it Zalamo [kizalamo], informant from Kisarawe. No dialect split is at issue.

sources.note: Lists Zaramo [G33] (with Kutu, Kami, Kwere, Swahili etc.) among the few Bantu languages lacking a binary tonal contrast; says nothing about where stress falls in Zaramo.

Group-related statements elsewhere: Lugulu (PT68) 'there is no lexical tone, no tone classes, and two tones: high and low. In general, nominals have a high on the first syllable of the stem...'; Makonde (PT110) '...similar to that of the Zaramo group in many languages, and we had some difficulty in determining whether to call this stress or tone.'
